newsitem.title: USA: INTERVIEW - P&G sees $100 mln savings in deal.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW - P&G sees $100 mln savings in deal.

text.p: Procter & Gamble Co said Wednesday it expects to reap about $100 million in annual savings within three years from its acquisition of Tambrands Inc, with some savings reaped in the first year.

"There is certainly going to be savings in the first year because there are certain redundant administrative costs, selling costs that will be eliminated fairly quickly," Clayton Daley Jr., vice president and treasurer, said in a telephone interview. "Other things will take a little more time to get to."

Other savings will come over time as Procter & Gamble applies its efficient consumer response (ECR) initiatives to Tambrands and its Tampax tampon. ECR includes efforts such as continuous product replenishment, just-in-time inventory management and more efficient promotions and assortment.
"We're a very big proponent of ECR," Daley said.
He said several changes will be needed to implement ECR at Tambrands. "They are a heavy user of promotions," Daley said.
Cost savings are expected to help make Procter & Gamble's $1.85 billion acquisition of Tambrands accretive in the second year and beyond, Daley said.
He reiterated the deal is expected to cut earnings by $0.02 to $0.03 a share in the first year, but that the company will strive to offset that dilution internally.

Earlier, analysts applauded Procter & Gamble's proposed acquisition of Tambrands for $50 a share. In particular, analysts said Procter & Gamble could expand marketing of Tampax in emerging nations. About 90 percent of Tampax's business currently is in North America and Europe.
"You might think of the U.S. and Europe as the financial drivers behind the deal, short-term," Daley said. "Long term, the opportunities are in developing markets."
The problem Procter & Gamble may face, however, is the difficulty of promoting Tampax in some cultures where discussing a feminine hygiene product may be a taboo.

"The (cultural) differences are critical. With a feminine hygiene products like tampons, it may be a touchy subject in some markets," Pradeep Chintagunta, professor of marketing at the University of Chicago, Graduate School of Business, said.
Daley acknowledged that expanding in emerging markets will require investments in school programs, product sampling, marketing and consumer education.

"In my view, it is going to take quite a while to reeducate consumers in the emerging markets into using tampons," JP Morgan analyst Michael Grant added. "P&G has the marketing know-how and the money to make that happen."
Daley said his company has reaped success in overseas markets with products like its Whisper feminine pad in Asia and Pantene hair care products.
For established markets, Procter & Gamble will increase development spending behind Tampax, Daley added.
While antitrust clearance for the Tambrands acquisition is not completely assured, the deal is expected to be approved, Daley said. "We are confident from an antitrust standpoint."
